course of instruction. The trustees their re-
port say: "Our efforts at further develop-
ment must be more or less cramped, until the
system here, as in other cities, is rounded out
and perfected by such an institution." Super-
intendent Wilson recommends that the fund
to endow public schools, which, with the inter-
est, now amounts to $50,900, be used to purchase
site and erect building for this school. Our
city has made wonderful progress in the
way of school buildings and educational
facilities generally, within the past ten years,
but there is yet room for still further improve-
ment. There is no good reason, as the superin-
tendent says, why our public schools should not
keep pace with the progress of the capital in
other respects; why, in fact, they should not
even outstrip, in point of excellence, those of
any other city in the Union. There is no valid
reason either why Congress should not aid
education in the District of Columbia, as it has
aided it in the territories.


Mr. Wilson does not believe in the common
notion that young and inexperienced teachers
should be selected teachers in primary
schools, and regrets that the scale of salaries is
frequently arranged to conform to that idea.
He thinks it far preferable to place in charge
of such schools teachers of well-known ability
and experience, and let the inexperienced be
employed in the second grade. This plan has
been tried and works very satisfactorily. In
regard to the relative efficiency of male and
female teachers, he says: "We have, thus far
in our experience, found female teachers to be
quite as competent as male teachers, and, in
some respects, better adapted to the work of
teaching."


The recommendation that all the school
boards flour in number in the District work
under some general system is worthy of consid-
eration, since, as he says, three of boards are
not clothed with sufficient powers to enable
them to manage school affairs with the highest
degree of efficiency, and the amount of school
tax now depends entirely upon the whim or
caprice of the District legislature. This change
he believes would insure greater economy in
the expenditures, a higher degree of efficiency
in the management of the schools, and more
rapid progress in developing them.


The reports in question, while they form
very gratifying exhibit of the condition of our
public schools, show that those directly charged
with their care are not presumptuous enough to
believe that they have reached absolute perfec-
tion, and that they are desirous of instituting
any improvements which will place Washing-
ton in advance of, or at least on a par with, any
other city in the world in respect to facilities
for popular education. For the earnest zeal

they have manifested, and for the gratifying

results of their labors in behalf of the public

schools, the Board of Trustees and the Super-
intendent merit the warmest recognition of the
community.

want to make my WILL' and then he dic-
tated it to me. I wrote it out for him.
He said, 'I am W. Little, the omnibus
man,' and then he went on and told me what
to write as calmly and coolly as if he was
sitting comfortably in an easy chair. Take
my studs and my pin, my watch and chain,
and don't let anybody have them but my
wife.' I did as he told me, and here you
see his two diamond studs, his pin, and

from others please go and look after some-
body else.' He was a man, William Little;
clear grit right through. And he is dead."

And then, afterwards, when the interests were consolidated, did they not tell him that they had made a mistake—that his claim was No. 7 instead of No. 4? And when they returned to Salt Lake all interests in the Panaca location centered in the Box family. They couldn't get a record book of any one else but Box, and they couldn't make their records anywhere else but in Box's house. They swindled old man Shirts out of his claim, and they know it. Shut, who had never stuck pick in the ground for the purpose of mining, and who was under the control of Box, was made the Deputy Recorder. He was brother Mormon. Here Judge Pitzer was informed that Shut was not Mormon; he replied that whether he was or not, he was controlled by Box. Testimony shows that in 1864 there were but three stakes stuck—one near what they call discovery shaft; one 150 feet from bounds of Hamlin's ground. The 800 feet were stepped off to the north to Hamlin by Sherwood, and then Sherwood measured off his own ground. Now, was there ever a pick stuck in the claim that is marked in their record as discovery claim? Their shaft that they worked in was south of the discovery claim. The Mormon policy, through Box, controlled after they returned to Salt Lake. They have got Gentiles with them, and they must take back enough Mormons on their return to locate the whole country, to override Gentile influence, and to secure to themselves the bulk of the silver. They had thrown oil at man Shirts overheard, and now they are ready to consolidate. But HIM Pulsifer would not sign the consolidation contract, when solicited to do so. Why? because he says to Hamlin, "I owned as much of that ground a year ago as you did, but now, and without your buying or my selling, you own 800 feet to my 50." And finally rather than be associated with such men—rather than place himself in their power—he gives Hamlin deed for his interest. But Pulsifer never did sign the consolidation agreement, and his 50 feet, on which the work was all done, never was in the consolidation. Every lick they struck was on the Pulsifer ground, and not a lick was struck elsewhere until 1870. Bish was wrong in calling the Panaca location a "galvanized corpse"; it never had enough vitality to become a corpse. Discovery, notices of location, and records are three things absolutely necessary to establishing mining claim. What can you make out of the notices of the Panaca location? Their diagram and the reading of their notices agree that they thought the stakes were set in the direction of the ledge. They made east and west cross-cuts to strike the ledge. Would they have done that if they did not think the ledge was north and south? And for several years all they did was making those cuts. A bloody campaign ensued, and one white man, named Rogers, was killed forty or fifty miles away. That was the extent of the mortality, with the exception that five Indians, while in their hands as captives, and under their complete control, were slaughtered.
